# Overlapping histograms {#sec-overlapping-histograms}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
# fonts ----
library(extrafont)
library(sysfonts)
source("_common.R")
# use font
showtext::showtext_auto()
# set theme
ggplot2::theme_set(fmggp2::theme_tamagotchi(
    base_size = 15))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Theme: `theme_tamagotchi()`

Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_tamagotchi()`, modeled on a Tamagotchi: a lilac egg shell, a gray green LCD screen plot area, pink, teal, and yellow shell colors, and a Futura title.
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}

<br>

```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1997)
tamagotchi_pets <- tibble(
  pet_id = 1:450,
  care = rep(c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered"), each = 150)) |>
  mutate(care = factor(care, levels = c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered")),
         lifespan_days = round(rweibull(n(), shape = 2.2,
           scale = c(Neglected = 6, Average = 13,
                     Pampered = 21)[as.character(care)]), 1))
labs_ovrlp_hist <- labs(
  title = "Tamagotchi lifespans",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "450 virtual pets and how they were cared for",
  x = "Lifespan (days)",
  fill = "Care")
ggp2_ovrlp_hist <- ggplot(data = tamagotchi_pets,
     aes(x = lifespan_days,
         fill = care)) +
     geom_histogram(alpha = 2/3, position = "identity", bins = 40)
ggp2_ovrlp_hist +
  labs_ovrlp_hist
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"}
**Requirements:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a categorical variable**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a numeric (continuous) variable**
:::

::::

## Description

Overlapping histograms put one [histogram](histograms.qmd) for each group in the same graph, one on top of the other. This lets us compare the form the numbers take[^dist-shape] from one group to the next.[^groups]

## Set up

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::


Bring in the code we'll use.[^packages]


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_ovrlp_hist
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

A pet is a dog or other small friend that people keep and care for. A Tamagotchi is a small computer you hold in your hand, with a pet inside it that is not real. In 1997, kids all over were giving food to, cleaning, and playing with their Tamagotchis, and how long a pet lived[^lifespan] turned on how well it was cared for. We'll make up[^simulate] 450 pets, 150 for each level of care. `rweibull()` picks how long each pet lives from a [rule made for how long things last](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weibull_distribution),[^weibull] and the `scale` for each level of care (6, 13, or 21 days) makes the lives of better cared for pets longer. Starting with `set.seed()`[^seed] means you'll get the same 450 pets every time you run the code below.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_ovrlp_hist
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1997) # same 450 pets every time the code runs
tamagotchi_pets <- tibble(
  pet_id = 1:450, # 450 different pets, one row each
  care = rep(c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered"), each = 150) # 150 pets for each level of care
  ) |>
  mutate(
    care = factor(care, levels = c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered")), # least to most care
    lifespan_days = round(
      rweibull(n(), shape = 2.2, # lifespans pile up in the middle
        scale = c(Neglected = 6, Average = 13, # typical lifespan in days
                  Pampered = 21)[as.character(care)]), # (looked up for each level of care)
      1 # one decimal place
      )
    )
glimpse(tamagotchi_pets)
```
:::

## Distribution

Overlapping histograms compare the form of one column from group to group. Here the groups all have the same *kind* of form (they all come from the same rule),[^same-dist] but each one is made wider by a different amount. Below we'll move from the pets, to a graph, to the rule behind it.[^formula]

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first five pets (all neglected).

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_values_ovrlp_hist
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
head(tamagotchi_pets, 5)
```
:::

None of these neglected pets lived past 9 days. The numbers below compare the three levels of care.[^summary] The median is the middle number when you put all the numbers in order. Each mean is a little higher than its median, and the pet that lived longest in each group lived more than two times as long as the median.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_summary_ovrlp_hist
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
tamagotchi_pets |> 
  group_by(care) |> 
  summarise(
    mean = mean(lifespan_days), 
    median = median(lifespan_days), 
    max = max(lifespan_days))
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

The histograms below are on top of each other (`position = "identity"`).[^identity] The lines show the rule we used to make up each group's lives, made big enough to match the bars.[^scaled] A hill is a line that is high in the middle and low on both sides. Every group makes the same hill, with one side that runs out farther to the right.[^skew] Better care doesn't change the form; it moves the hill to the right, makes it wider, and makes it lower.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_ovrlp_hist
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
weibull_curves <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  care = factor(c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered"), 
    levels = c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered")),
  lifespan_days = seq(0, 45, by = 0.25)) |> 
  mutate(scale = c(Neglected = 6, Average = 13, 
                   Pampered = 21)[as.character(care)],
         count = 150 * (45 / 40) * dweibull(lifespan_days, 
           shape = 2.2, scale = scale))

ggplot(data = tamagotchi_pets, aes(x = lifespan_days, fill = care)) + 
  geom_histogram(alpha = 2/3, position = "identity", 
    binwidth = 45 / 40, boundary = 0) + 
  geom_line(data = weibull_curves, aes(y = count, color = care), 
    linewidth = 1, show.legend = FALSE) + 
  labs(x = "Lifespan (days)", y = "Pets", fill = "Care")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

The [rule we used](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weibull_distribution)[^weibull-name] is often used for how long things last. It has two numbers in it:[^params] a `shape` ($k$) and a `scale` ($\lambda$):

$$
X \sim \text{Weibull}(k = 2.2, \; \lambda_{\text{care}}), \quad \lambda = (6, 13, 21)
$$

The chance that a pet is still living after $t$ days is $e^{-(t/\lambda)^k}$. When `shape` is more than 1 (like our 2.2), the chance that a pet dies gets bigger the longer it lives,[^hazard] which gives the histogram its hill and its long side to the right. `scale` moves everything to the right and makes it wider: the median life is $\lambda (\ln 2)^{1/k}$, which is about 5, 11, and 18 days for our three groups. The medians of the pets we made up are `r paste(round(tapply(tamagotchi_pets$lifespan_days, tamagotchi_pets$care, median), 1), collapse = ", ")` days. 

Try changing `shape` in `rweibull()`. A `shape` of 1 turns the hill into bars that only get shorter (a pet is as likely to die on any day, no matter how old it is),[^exponential] and a large `shape` makes every pet in a group die at about the same time.


## Grammar

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::


  -   Make the words around the graph[^labels] with `labs()`

  -   Start the graph with `ggplot()` and give it `data`

  -   Put `lifespan_days` on the `x` axis, and give each level of `care` its own color with `fill`

  -   Inside `geom_histogram()`, set `alpha` to `2/3` (so we can see through the bars), `position` to `"identity"` (so each group's bars start at 0 and cover each other, instead of starting where the last group's bars end),[^stack] and `bins` to `40`

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_ovrlp_hist
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
labs_ovrlp_hist <- labs(
  title = "Tamagotchi lifespans",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "450 virtual pets and how they were cared for",
  x = "Lifespan (days)",
  fill = "Care")
ggp2_ovrlp_hist <- ggplot(data = tamagotchi_pets,
     aes(x = lifespan_days,
         fill = care)) +
     geom_histogram(alpha = 2/3, position = "identity", bins = 40)
ggp2_ovrlp_hist +
  labs_ovrlp_hist
```
:::



::: {.column-margin}
Try different values of `binwidth` when you compare the form of the numbers across groups.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

Histograms work by cutting the column we put on `x` [*into bins and counting the number of observations in each bin.*](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_histogram.html)

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
```{r}
#| label: create_graph_ovrlp_hist
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_ovrlp_hist <- labs(
  title = "Tamagotchi lifespans",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "450 virtual pets and how they were cared for",
  x = "Lifespan (days)",
  fill = "Care")
ggp2_ovrlp_hist <- ggplot(data = tamagotchi_pets,
     aes(x = lifespan_days,
         fill = care)) +
     geom_histogram(alpha = 2/3, position = "identity", bins = 40)
ggp2_ovrlp_hist +
  labs_ovrlp_hist
```
:::

[^dist-shape]: The shape of the variable's distribution.

[^groups]: The groups of a categorical (or ordinal) variable.

[^packages]: Install and load the packages.

[^lifespan]: Its lifespan.

[^simulate]: Simulate.

[^weibull]: A Weibull distribution, a common model for lifetimes.

[^seed]: Setting the random seed.

[^same-dist]: The same distribution (Weibull, with the same shape).

[^formula]: The formula.

[^summary]: Summary statistics: the mean, median, and maximum for each group.

[^identity]: With `position = "identity"`, the histograms overlap instead of stacking.

[^scaled]: The Weibull density curves, scaled to counts (150 pets × bin width × density).

[^skew]: A lopsided (right skewed) hump with a tail to the right.

[^weibull-name]: The Weibull distribution.

[^params]: Its parameters.

[^hazard]: The hazard (risk of dying) increases with age.

[^exponential]: A shape of 1 is the exponential distribution: a steady decline with a constant hazard.

[^labels]: Labels.

[^stack]: The default for `geom_histogram()` is `position = "stack"`, which piles the groups on top of each other.
